client: I've been struggling a lot since my grandmother passed away last month. The sadness just kind of sits on my chest all day, and I keep finding myself wondering what the point of everything is — like, what am I even working toward anymore. I'm not sure talking about it is really going to change anything, but I figured I'd give this a shot.
therapist: I'm really glad you gave this a shot, and I want you to know that what you're carrying sounds genuinely heavy — grief has a way of quietly pulling the meaning out of everyday things, and that weight on your chest makes a lot of sense given what you've been through. It's also completely okay to feel uncertain about whether talking will help; that doubt doesn't have to go away before we can make some progress together. I'm curious — when you ask yourself "what's the point," are there any specific areas of your life, like work, relationships, or daily routines, where that feeling hits the hardest?

client: Honestly, it hits hardest with my friendships, or I guess what used to be my friendships. Since my dad passed, I've kind of pulled back from everyone, and now it feels like too much time has gone by to just pick up where we left off, so I don't even try. It's like I'm waiting for someone to reach out first, but they don't, and that just confirms this feeling that I'm basically alone in this.
therapist: It sounds like grief has quietly built a wall between you and the people who might actually want to be there for you, and that silence from others is getting interpreted as confirmation that you don't matter to them — which is such a painful place to be stuck. I want to gently notice something: the thought "too much time has passed" might be acting like a rule that's protecting you from potential hurt, but also keeping you from testing whether it's actually true. What do you imagine might happen if one of those friends *did* hear from you — what's the story you tell yourself about how they'd respond?

client: I think they'd probably be polite but distant, like... they'd respond out of obligation, not because they actually missed me. And then I'd know for sure that I waited too long and ruined it, which almost feels worse than just not knowing. At least right now I can tell myself maybe they still care, but if I reach out and get that lukewarm response, that hope is just gone.
therapist: There's something really understandable about protecting that last bit of hope — it feels safer to hold onto "maybe" than to risk a painful answer. But I want to gently point out that your mind has already decided the outcome will be lukewarm, and that prediction is quietly doing the same damage as the rejection you're trying to avoid — it's already making you feel alone. I'm wondering, is there a friend from that time who, if you're really honest with yourself, you'd be the most surprised to get a cold response from?

client: I mean... yeah, there's this one guy, Marcus. We used to talk almost every day back in college, and he was always the kind of person who actually showed up, you know? But that's almost what makes it scarier — if I reached out to Marcus and he gave me some polite, distant response, I think that would hurt way more than if it came from someone I wasn't as close to.
therapist: It's really meaningful that Marcus came to mind so quickly — the fact that he was someone who *actually showed up* suggests your instinct about him isn't just wishful thinking, it's based on real evidence of who he is. The fear makes complete sense, but I want to reflect something back: you're essentially protecting yourself from losing someone you may have already convinced yourself you've lost, when Marcus might be sitting on his side wondering the same thing about you. What do you think the Marcus you knew back then would say if he knew you'd been going through all of this grief alone?

client: That question kind of stopped me for a second, because honestly... the Marcus I knew back then would probably be annoyed that I didn't call him sooner. He was always the type to say "why didn't you tell me" after the fact, like he genuinely wanted to be included in the hard stuff. But then I start thinking, that was years ago, and people change, and maybe I'm just romanticizing who he was because I'm lonely and desperate for it to be that simple.
therapist: That moment of pause feels really important — because what you just described wasn't romanticizing, it was *remembering*, and there's a difference. You have actual, specific evidence of who Marcus was: someone who wanted to be included in the hard stuff and would have shown up. The thought "people change" is worth examining, but notice it's doing a lot of work right now to talk you out of something your gut seems to already know. What would it mean about you — not about Marcus — if you let yourself act on what you actually remember rather than the worst-case version you've imagined?

client: That question kind of stops me in my tracks, honestly. Like, if I act on what I actually remember about Marcus and it goes well, maybe that means I've been the one keeping myself isolated all this time — and that's a hard thing to sit with. It's easier to tell myself people change or they won't show up than to admit I might be the one pushing them away before they get the chance.
therapist: What you just said takes real courage to admit, and I want you to sit with the fact that recognizing a pattern isn't the same as being at fault — it's actually the first step toward changing it. The story "I push people away to protect myself" is painful, but it's also genuinely hopeful, because unlike "people don't care," it's something *you* have power over. If that protective part of you that pulls back could speak honestly, what do you think it's most afraid would happen if you let someone like Marcus actually back in?

client: I think that part of me is afraid that if I let Marcus back in, he'll eventually see how much of a mess I really am and just... leave anyway. And then it won't just be loneliness, it'll be proof that I was right not to trust anyone in the first place. At least right now I can tell myself it's my choice to be alone, but if I try and he still goes, I don't know how I'd come back from that.
therapist: What you're describing is such a deeply human fear — that being truly *seen* is the most dangerous thing of all, because then any rejection feels like a verdict on your worth rather than just a circumstance. I want to gently reflect that the "mess" you're afraid Marcus will see is someone who has lost two important people and is still trying to find their way back — and that's not a reason to leave someone, for most people that's actually a reason to stay closer. I'm curious, if a close friend came to you and said exactly what you just said to me — "I'm a mess and I'm afraid of being abandoned" — what would you feel toward them, and would it make you want to pull away?

client: I'd feel really sad for them, and I'd want to be there for them more, not less. But I know what you're trying to do with that question, and I get it logically — I just can't seem to apply that same compassion to myself when it comes to Marcus. It's like there's this wall between understanding something intellectually and actually believing it when it's about me.
therapist: The fact that you can see the wall so clearly actually matters more than it might feel like right now — a lot of people never even get that far, and you're already standing right in front of it. That gap between "I understand this" and "I can feel it about myself" is one of the most common and honest struggles in grief, and it doesn't mean you're broken or that the compassion isn't in you — it just means it's been turned outward for so long that pointing it inward feels almost foreign. I wonder, what do you think it would take — even just a small step — to start treating yourself a little more like the friend you'd want to show up for?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it... but honestly, when I try to imagine treating myself like a friend, it just feels kind of hollow, like I'm going through the motions without really meaning it. I think the obstacle is that I don't feel like I deserve that kind of care right now, especially after how things ended with my dad — like there's still so much guilt sitting on top of everything. It's hard to extend warmth to yourself when part of you thinks you don't really earn it.
therapist: The guilt you're describing feels like it might be quietly running a lot of this — like it's the deeper layer underneath the isolation and the fear with Marcus, and it makes sense that self-compassion would feel hollow if part of you believes you don't deserve to receive it yet. I want to hold space for that guilt without rushing past it, because it sounds like it's carrying something important about your relationship with your dad. Would you be willing to share a little about what happened there — not to judge it, but because I think understanding what you're holding might help us figure out what that guilt is actually asking of you?

client: I've never really talked about this out loud before, so it feels strange to even start. My dad got sick a few years ago, and I kept telling myself I'd visit more, call more, but I always had some reason not to — work, or I was stressed, or we'd had another argument and I needed space. And then he died before I ever really made it right, and I've been carrying that ever since.
therapist: Thank you for trusting me with something you've never said out loud before — that takes real courage, and I want you to know there's no judgment here, only care. What you're describing is something so many people carry in silence: the painful collision of ordinary life — stress, conflict, distance — with a loss that came before the reconciliation you were hoping for. I want to gently ask: when you imagine "making it right" with your dad, what does that actually look like to you — what is it you most wish he could have known?
